background:
1 Thessalonians: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

1 Thessalonians is one of the earliest books of the New Testament, written around AD 50–51, only about twenty years after Jesus' resurrection. Paul encourages a young, persecuted church and answers their questions about believers who have died before Christ's return.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul, with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy (1:1)Accepted by virtually all scholars as Paul's.
DateAbout AD 50–51Possibly the earliest surviving Christian writing, unless Galatians is earlier.
Written fromCorinthTimothy had just returned from Thessalonica with good news (3:6; Acts 18:5).
RecipientsThe church in ThessalonicaMostly Gentiles who had “turned unto God from idols” (1:9); some Jews and God-fearing Greeks (Acts 17:4).
BackgroundPaul was forced to leave after a few weeksA mob attacked Jason's house, and the believers sent Paul away by night (Acts 17:5–10).
Key themeThe coming (parousia) of the LordEvery chapter ends with a reference to Christ's return.

The letter has two parts: Paul's thanksgiving and relationship with them (1–3), and instructions for holy living and hope (4–5).

The time map

The shaded band marks AD 50–51, during Paul's eighteen months in Corinth. Claudius had recently expelled the Jews from Rome.

Rome and Thessalonica

Thessalonica owed its privileges to Rome and honored the emperors gladly, which made a message about “another king” dangerous (Acts 17:7).

  • A free city. Thessalonica had backed Antony and Octavian in 42 BC and was rewarded with the status of a free city, governing itself under Rome's protection.
  • Politarchs. Its officials, called politarchs (Acts 17:6), are named in inscriptions found in the city.
  • Emperor worship. The city built a temple to Augustus and minted coins calling Julius Caesar a god. Honoring the emperors was a civic duty.
  • “Peace and safety.” Roman propaganda celebrated the pax and securitas the empire brought. Paul warns that when people say “Peace and safety,” sudden destruction will come (5:3).
  • Imperial visits. When an emperor or official visited a city, leading citizens went out to meet him and escort him in. Paul uses the same words, “coming” and “meet,” for Christ's return (4:15–17).
  • Claudius. Claudius was emperor. The charge that Christians acted “contrary to the decrees of Caesar” (Acts 17:7) may refer to his decrees against predictions about rulers.

Turning from idols to “a living and true God” (1:9) meant leaving the city's gods and civic religion, which brought hostility from neighbors (2:14).

Thessalonica

Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and its largest city, a port on the Via Egnatia.

  • Size and trade. A busy port of perhaps 40,000–100,000 people, where the Via Egnatia met the sea lanes of the Aegean.
  • Religions. Inscriptions show worship of Egyptian gods, Dionysus and especially the local god Cabirus, along with the emperors.
  • Jewish community. A synagogue where Paul reasoned for three Sabbaths (Acts 17:1–3).
  • Working believers. Paul worked “night and day” to support himself (2:9) and urged believers to work with their hands (4:11), perhaps in workshops where they lived and labored.
  • Persecution. The church suffered from their own countrymen (2:14), and Paul's quick departure left them anxious.
  • Influence. Their faith became known throughout Macedonia and Achaia (1:7–8), helped by the city's position on major routes.

Around the world in AD 50–51

When Paul wrote, Claudius ruled Rome.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainRoman conquest continued after Claudius' invasion of AD 43. The British leader Caratacus was captured in AD 51 and paraded in Rome, where Claudius pardoned him.
RomeClaudius was poisoned in AD 54, most likely by his wife Agrippina, and her 16-year-old son Nero became emperor, guided by the philosopher Seneca.
Armenia and ParthiaFrom AD 58 Rome's general Corbulo fought the Parthians over Armenia, a war that lasted until AD 63.
JudeaUnrest grew under the governors Felix and Festus, with bandits, assassins (the sicarii) and false prophets.
EgyptAlexandria shipped Egypt's grain to Rome every year; its huge Jewish community had survived riots under Caligula.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming (AD 57–75). Tradition says Buddhism arrived in his reign.
IndiaRoman ships sailed to southern India with the monsoon winds for pepper; Roman coins have been found there.
The AmericasTeotihuacan near Mexico City was growing into one of the world's great cities.

How the setting shapes the study

Several phrases in 1 Thessalonians echo the political language of the day.

PassageConnection to the times
1 Thess 1:9Turning from idols meant leaving the city's gods, including the cult of the emperors.
1 Thess 1:10Jesus “delivereth us from the wrath to come,” while Rome offered deliverance by its power.
1 Thess 2:7Paul compares himself to a nursing mother, unlike popular orators who sought money and fame.
1 Thess 2:9Paul worked at his trade rather than take money from the believers.
1 Thess 2:14“Your own countrymen”: local Gentiles stirred up opposition (Acts 17:5).
1 Thess 4:15–17“Coming” and “meet” were used for welcoming a visiting emperor or official.
1 Thess 5:3“Peace and safety” echoes Rome's slogans of pax and securitas.
1 Thess 5:8The armor of faith, love and hope; Roman soldiers were a familiar sight on the Via Egnatia.
1 Thess 5:27Letters were read aloud to the whole church, since many could not read.

In a city that celebrated the visits of Caesar, Paul taught believers to wait for the coming of the true Lord.

Maps: then and now

Paul traveled west along the Via Egnatia from Philippi to Thessalonica, about 90 miles, then fled to Berea and went on by sea or road to Athens and Corinth.

Today Thessalonica is Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city. Its Roman forum and the later Arch of Galerius can be seen downtown.

items.text: The Thessalonians' Faith and Example
Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, unto the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
We give thanks to God always for you all, making mention of you in our prayers;
remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labor of love and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father;
knowing, brethren beloved of God, your election,
how that our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much assurance; even as ye know what manner of men we showed ourselves toward you for your sake.
And ye became imitators of us, and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit;
so that ye became an ensample to all that believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
For from you hath sounded forth the word of the Lord, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith to God-ward is gone forth; so that we need not to speak anything.
For they themselves report concerning us what manner of entering in we had unto you; and how ye turned unto God from idols, to serve a living and true God,
and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, even Jesus, who delivereth us from the wrath to come.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the church and thank God constantly for their “work of faith and labor of love and patience of hope” in Jesus Christ. They know God chose them, because the gospel came to them not only in word but in power, in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction.

Though they received the word in much affliction, they did so with joy from the Holy Spirit and became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Everywhere people report how they “turned unto God from idols, to serve a living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven,” Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What three qualities does Paul remember in verse 3, and how did the Thessalonians receive the word according to verses 5–6?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: What would it have cost people in Thessalonica, a busy Roman city full of temples, to turn to God from idols (v. 9)?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: The Thessalonians became an example that others talked about (vv. 7–8); what story might people around you tell about your community's faith?

items.text: Paul's Ministry in Thessalonica
For yourselves, brethren, know our entering in unto you, that it hath not been found vain:
but having suffered before and been shamefully treated, as ye know, at Philippi, we waxed bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God in much conflict.
For our exhortation is not of error, nor of uncleanness, nor in guile:
but even as we have been approved of God to be intrusted with the gospel, so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God who proveth our hearts.
For neither at any time were we found using words of flattery, as ye know, nor a cloak of covetousness, God is witness;
nor seeking glory of men, neither from you nor from others, when we might have claimed authority as apostles of Christ.
But we were gentle in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherisheth her own children:
even so, being affectionately desirous of you, we were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us.
For ye remember, brethren, our labor and travail: working night and day, that we might not burden any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God.
Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and righteously and unblamably we behaved ourselves toward you that believe:
as ye know how we dealt with each one of you, as a father with his own children, exhorting you, and encouraging you, and testifying,
to the end that ye should walk worthily of God, who calleth you into his own kingdom and glory.
Receiving God's Word Amid Suffering

And for this cause we also thank God without ceasing, that, when ye received from us the word of the message, even the word of God, ye accepted it not as the word of men, but, as it is in truth, the word of God, which also worketh in you that believe.
For ye, brethren, became imitators of the churches of God which are in Judæa in Christ Jesus: for ye also suffered the same things of your own countrymen, even as they did of the Jews;
who both killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove out us, and please not God, and are contrary to all men;
forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they may be saved; to fill up their sins always: but the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost.
Paul's Longing to See Them
But we, brethren, being bereaved of you for a short season, in presence not in heart, endeavored the more exceedingly to see your face with great desire:
because we would fain have come unto you, I Paul once and again; and Satan hindered us.
For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glorying? Are not even ye, before our Lord Jesus at his coming?
For ye are our glory and our joy.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul reminds them of his visit. After being shamefully treated at Philippi, he boldly preached the gospel in Thessalonica despite opposition, not from deceit or to please men, nor seeking glory or money. He was gentle among them like a nursing mother, and worked night and day so as not to be a burden, exhorting each one like a father to walk worthily of God.

He thanks God that they received his message as the word of God, which is at work in them. They suffered from their countrymen just as the Judean churches suffered from those who killed the Lord Jesus and drove out Paul. Since being torn away from them, Paul has longed to see them; Satan hindered him, but they are his glory and joy at the Lord's coming.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: Which images does Paul use for his ministry in verses 7 and 11, and what does each suggest about how he treated the believers?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why did Paul stress that he worked night and day and took no money (v. 9), when wandering teachers in Greek cities often sought payment and praise?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul shared not only the gospel but his own life (v. 8); what would sharing your life, not just your words, look like with someone this month?

items.text: Timothy's Encouraging Report
Wherefore when we could no longer forbear, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone;
and sent Timothy, our brother and God’s minister in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith;
that no man be moved by these afflictions; for yourselves know that hereunto we are appointed.
For verily, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we are to suffer affliction; even as it came to pass, and ye know.
For this cause I also, when I could no longer forbear, sent that I might know your faith, lest by any means the tempter had tempted you, and our labor should be in vain.
But when Timothy came even now unto us from you, and brought us glad tidings of your faith and love, and that ye have good remembrance of us always, longing to see us, even as we also to see you;
for this cause, brethren, we were comforted over you in all our distress and affliction through your faith:
for now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord.
For what thanksgiving can we render again unto God for you, for all the joy wherewith we joy for your sakes before our God;
night and day praying exceedingly that we may see your face, and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith?
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way unto you:
and the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we also do toward you;
to the end he may establish your hearts unblamable in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

notes.label: CONNECTION TO THE TIMES

parts.text: Timothy had been sent from Athens and returned to Paul at Corinth (Acts 18:5).

notes.text: Timothy had been sent from Athens and returned to Paul at Corinth (Acts 18:5).

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: Unable to bear the uncertainty, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen and encourage them, so that no one would be shaken by afflictions, which he had warned them would come. He feared the tempter might have undone his work.

Now Timothy has returned with good news of their faith and love and their desire to see Paul, and Paul is comforted in all his distress: “for now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord.” He prays night and day to see them, and asks the Lord to make them increase and abound in love for one another and for all, and to establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: Why did Paul send Timothy according to verses 1–5, and how did Timothy's report change Paul's outlook (vv. 6–10)?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: How would the Thessalonians have heard Paul's reminder that afflictions were expected (vv. 3–4) after he had been forced out of their city so quickly?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul prays that love would increase toward one another and toward all (v. 12); whom outside your usual circle might that love need to reach?

items.text: A Life Pleasing to God
Finally then, brethren, we beseech and exhort you in the Lord Jesus, that, as ye received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, even as ye do walk,—that ye abound more and more.
For ye know what charge we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye abstain from fornication;
that each one of you know how to possess himself of his own vessel in sanctification and honor,
not in the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who know not God;
that no man transgress, and wrong his brother in the matter: because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as also we forewarned you and testified.
For God called us not for uncleanness, but in sanctification.
Therefore he that rejecteth, rejecteth not man, but God, who giveth his Holy Spirit unto you.
But concerning love of the brethren ye have no need that one write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another;
for indeed ye do it toward all the brethren that are in all Macedonia. But we exhort you, brethren, that ye abound more and more;
and that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your hands, even as we charged you;
that ye may walk becomingly toward them that are without, and may have need of nothing.
The Coming of the Lord
But we would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that fall asleep; that ye sorrow not, even as the rest, who have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also that are fallen asleep in Jesus will God bring with him.
For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we that are alive, that are left unto the coming of the Lord, shall in no wise precede them that are fallen asleep.
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven, with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first;
then we that are alive, that are left, shall together with them be caught up in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
Wherefore comfort one another with these words.

summary.title: CHAPTER 4 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul urges them to keep living to please God, as they have been taught. God's will is their sanctification: to abstain from sexual immorality and control their bodies in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion like Gentiles who do not know God. They need no instruction about loving one another, but should do so more and more, aspiring to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands.

Some believers have died, and the church is grieving. Paul does not want them to grieve “even as the rest, who have no hope.” Since Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep. “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven, with a shout,” the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air, “and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words.”

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What does Paul say about those who have fallen asleep in verses 13–18, and what comfort does he draw from the Lord's coming?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: In a Greco-Roman culture where sexual freedom was often expected of men, how countercultural were Paul's instructions about holiness in verses 3–8?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul urges a quiet life, minding your own affairs and working with your hands (v. 11); how might that calling look in your daily routine?

items.text: The Day of the Lord
But concerning the times and the seasons, brethren, ye have no need that aught be written unto you.
For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night.
When they are saying, Peace and safety, then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall in no wise escape.
But ye, brethren, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you as a thief:
for ye are all sons of light, and sons of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness;
so then let us not sleep, as do the rest, but let us watch and be sober.
For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that are drunken are drunken in the night.
But let us, since we are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for a helmet, the hope of salvation.
For God appointed us not unto wrath, but unto the obtaining of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,
who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him.
Wherefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as also ye do.
Final Instructions and Blessing
But we beseech you, brethren, to know them that labor among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you;
and to esteem them exceeding highly in love for their work’s sake. Be at peace among yourselves.
And we exhort you, brethren, admonish the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be longsuffering toward all.
See that none render unto any one evil for evil; but always follow after that which is good, one toward another, and toward all.
Rejoice always;
pray without ceasing;
in everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus to you-ward.
Quench not the Spirit;
despise not prophesyings;
prove all things; hold fast that which is good;
abstain from every form of evil.
And the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved entire, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Faithful is he that calleth you, who will also do it.
Brethren, pray for us.
Salute all the brethren with a holy kiss.
I adjure you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the brethren.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

summary.title: CHAPTER 5 IN SUMMARY
paras: As for times and seasons, the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When people say, “Peace and safety,” sudden destruction will come. But believers are children of light and of the day, so they must stay awake and sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation, for God appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through Jesus Christ.

Paul ends with brief instructions: respect those who labor among them, be at peace, warn the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all, and never repay evil for evil. “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing; in everything give thanks.” Do not quench the Spirit, test everything and hold fast what is good. He prays that God would sanctify them completely, and asks that the letter be read to all the brothers.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What contrasts between day and night, sleep and watchfulness does Paul draw in verses 4–8, and what armor does he name?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why might the Roman slogan of peace and safety (v. 3) have given Paul's warning about sudden destruction particular force in Thessalonica?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Verses 12–22 give many brief commands; which one do you find hardest to practice, and what small step could you take toward it?

wrap.title: 1 Thessalonians In Summary
paras: 1 Thessalonians is a letter of encouragement to a young church. Paul had founded it only months earlier, but he was driven out of the city after a few weeks, leaving new believers to face persecution alone. When Timothy brought word that they were standing firm, Paul wrote with relief, thanksgiving and deep affection.

The letter shows what genuine conversion looks like. The Thessalonians “turned unto God from idols, to serve a living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven” (1:9–10), and their faith, love and hope became known far and wide. Paul's own example, gentle as a mother, hardworking and honest, shows what a true minister of the gospel looks like.

Paul also calls the church to holiness. In a city where sexual freedom was common, believers must control their bodies in honor, love one another more and more, and work quietly with their own hands, so that outsiders will respect them.

The best-known part of the letter answers a pastoral question: what happens to believers who die before Christ returns? Paul assures them that the dead in Christ will rise first, and all believers will be caught up together to meet the Lord and be with Him forever. Meanwhile the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, so believers must live as children of the light, alert and sober.

The message in one line: a church that has turned from idols to the living God can stand firm under pressure, live in holiness and love, and face death with hope, because the Lord Jesus is coming again and we shall always be with Him.
